title: Testing + Security + Observability + Performance
description: Turn production quality into observable, testable engineering rather than a checklist.

lessons.title: Testing by Risk and Boundary
lessons.why: Choose the cheapest test that proves the behavior at the correct boundary.
objectives: Explain Testing by Risk and Boundary using a concrete runtime/data-flow model.
Implement the smallest working example and predict its behavior before execution.
Diagnose a controlled failure related to Testing by Risk and Boundary using evidence rather than random edits.
Transfer the concept into the TaskFlow project without copying the finished example.
lessons.mentalModel: Turn production quality into observable, testable engineering rather than a checklist.
beforeYouCode: Open a scratch file or the relevant TaskFlow package.
Run the existing project/tests once so you know the baseline is healthy.
State what evidence will prove success before changing code.
steps: Write the goal in observable terms before coding: by the end of this lesson you should be able to demonstrate “Testing by Risk and Boundary” in a running TaskFlow-oriented example.
Read the example once without running it. Predict the exact output, state change, request, or compiler behavior and write that prediction down.
Type the example yourself rather than pasting it. Run the narrowest command that exercises only this concept, then compare observed evidence with your prediction.
Change one assumption at a time. Keep the change small enough that you can explain why the result changed.
Perform the intentional failure lab: Mock every dependency in every test and identify what integration failures become invisible.
Read the resulting compiler error, stack trace, HTTP response, browser evidence, database state, or CI log from the first line that is actually relevant to your code.
Repair only the root cause. Re-run the same verification so you can prove the repair changed the observed evidence.
Close the reference and rebuild the important part from memory. If you cannot explain why each boundary exists, revisit the smallest missing concept rather than memorizing the final code.

example.code:
unit: pure rule
integration: service + DB
API: HTTP contract
E2E: critical user journey
example.expected: Different test levels answer different questions; more E2E is not automatically better.

lessons.breakIt: Mock every dependency in every test and identify what integration failures become invisible.
debugChecklist: What did you predict?
What actually happened?
At what boundary do those first differ?
What is the smallest piece of evidence that proves the failure lives there?
Can you fix the cause without changing unrelated layers?
Can you add a regression test or repeatable verification?
lessons.challenge: Apply Testing by Risk and Boundary to one new TaskFlow requirement. Do not reopen the example until you have a failing attempt, an explanation of the failure, and a specific question you cannot answer.
exitTicket: I can explain why Testing by Risk and Boundary exists.
I can predict the example before running it.
I can reproduce the core behavior from memory.
I can create and diagnose the intentional failure.
I can name what would change in a production system.
